entities.summary:
Richard Rufus of Cornwall was a Cornish Franciscan scholastic philosopher and theologian active in the 13th century. Born in Cornwall, England, around 1220, he is believed to have studied at the University of Oxford and later became a prominent figure in the Franciscan movement. His scholarly works, including treatises on logic and theology, demonstrate his expertise in philosophical and theological debates of the time. Rufus's writings often engaged with the ideas of influential thinkers like Peter Abelard and John Duns Scotus. Despite his regional focus, Rufus's work had a lasting impact on the development of scholastic philosophy and the Franciscan Order. His legacy can be seen in the continued study and influence of his writings among Franciscan scholars and philosophers.

Rufus's life was marked by his dedication to the Franciscan cause, which led him to participate in the Third Council of Limoges in 1274. This event, which aimed to resolve disputes between the Franciscan and Dominican Orders, had significant implications for the future of the Franciscan movement. Rufus's involvement in this council reflects his commitment to the principles of the Franciscan Order and his desire to promote the unity of the Franciscan community.

In addition to his academic pursuits, Rufus was also a devout member of the Franciscan Order, which led him to establish a number of foundations and churches throughout Cornwall. His philanthropic efforts, while not widely documented, demonstrate his commitment to the welfare of his community and the Franciscan ideals of poverty, chastity, and obedience. Rufus's life serves as a testament to the enduring power of the Franciscan spirit, which continues to inspire scholars, theologians, and members of the Franciscan Order to this day.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Richard Rufus of Cornwall was a prominent figure in the Franciscan movement, whose scholarly works helped shape the Order's intellectual traditions and influenced the development of scholastic philosophy. His legacy continues to inspire scholars and thinkers across the centuries.
